q: Hypoglycaemia in an infant of a diabetic mother is due to:
e: Fetal hyperinsulinism continues after the supply of maternal glucose stops at birth.

q: The most specific congenital anomaly in an infant of a diabetic mother is:
e: Caudal regression is rare but the most specific anomaly of maternal diabetes.

q: All are complications of an infant of a diabetic mother EXCEPT:
e: Infants of diabetic mothers develop hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia.

q: A jittery infant of a diabetic mother has a glucose of 1.8 mmol/L and a seizure. What is the treatment?
o: 10% glucose 2 ml/kg intravenously, then an infusion
e: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia is treated with a bolus of intravenous 10% glucose, followed by 60–90 ml/kg/day.

q: A well infant of a diabetic mother has a glucose of 2.3 mmol/L at 3 hours and is feeding. What is the best step?
o: Feed and give 40% dextrose gel, then recheck
e: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia: a feed and 40% dextrose gel 0.5 ml/kg into the cheek, with a recheck in 30–60 minutes.

q: Late neonatal hypocalcaemia (end of the first week) is classically caused by:
e: The high phosphate load of cow's milk lowers the calcium.

q: Neonatal polycythaemia is defined as a venous haematocrit above:
e: A venous haematocrit above 65%; symptomatic babies need a partial exchange transfusion with saline.

q: A breastfed baby born at home without vitamin K has melaena on day 3; the platelets are normal and the prothrombin time is prolonged. What is the diagnosis?
e: Classic vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs on days 2–7 without prophylaxis, because breast milk is low in vitamin K.

q: Treatment of vitamin K deficiency bleeding is:
o: Vitamin K 1 mg intravenously (with fresh frozen plasma if the bleeding is serious)
e: Vitamin K corrects the clotting factors within hours; fresh frozen plasma is given for serious bleeding.

q: A well newborn vomits blood. The test to show it is maternal blood is:
e: Fetal haemoglobin resists alkali and stays pink; maternal haemoglobin turns brown.
